hero.headline: Hobe Sound couple seeks community support as husband battles head and neck cancer
hero.body:
A Hobe Sound couple is asking for community support as they navigate a cancer diagnosis, holding onto faith every step of the way. Dave and Faren Motz met in South Florida before moving to Maui, where they married and raised their three children. Faren homeschooled all three children and the couple started a farm business that served children. Years later, the couple moved to Hobe Sound and purchased a property, but just months after settling in, Dave was diagnosed with head and neck cancer.

As the couple searched for the right healthcare in Florida, AdventHealth in Celebration provided programs and grants that became a critical resource for them. Dave underwent nearly seven weeks of daily radiation treatments, with some days going better than others. The repeated visits to Orlando for radiation, biopsies, scans, and exams cost the couple nearly $20,000 out of pocket. Their age and income kept them from qualifying for Medicare or Medicaid. Faren said the catastrophic situation was exactly what the charity programs were designed to help with, crediting the kind donors who contributed to saving her husband's life.

Dave, a former firefighter, had long been the family's provider. Now Faren has stepped up to support them both as Dave focuses on recovery. Doctors told Dave he has an 85% chance of recovery. Dave praised his wife's strength throughout the ordeal, saying she got him through the surgery and drove him back and forth from Orlando. He expressed gratitude that he was the one facing cancer rather than watching Faren go through it, saying it would have been heartbreaking and questioning whether he would have had the strength to handle it. Through it all, the couple has leaned on their faith, with Faren saying their journey has been all about faith.

Their journey reflects their commitment to each other through the hardest days and the brighter ones ahead. Faren said she holds onto gratitude every day, constantly telling Dave how glad she is that he's here. Faren works at Latitudes at the Jupiter Beach Resort, where those who want to show their support can stop by and visit. Those who would like to contribute financially can donate to the family's GoFundMe at Standing with Dave Motz in his cancer battle.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie City Council rezones residential lot to commercial despite homeowner opposition
cards.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council voted unanimously Monday to rezone a residential lot behind the home of Margaret and Joseph Mucciolo to commercial use, despite the couple's months-long opposition. The Mucciolos purchased their Port St. Lucie home for the views of nature and quiet setting, with trees currently standing on the lot behind their yard. Margaret Mucciolo said she saw the beautiful setting and told the real estate agent to get ready to make an offer because it felt like home. Now they say their backyard and sense of quiet relaxation are under threat, with Joseph Mucciolo predicting that in six months or a year, the trees are going to be gone.

The council members said the change is necessary to reduce traffic in the neighborhood. One council member stated that adding commercial closer to neighborhoods reduces the length of trips, which reduces overall traffic because if you have commercial closer to you, your trips are shorter and it reduces the burden on the overall network. The Mucciolos have fought the rezoning for months, during which they feel their voices have gone unheard. Margaret Mucciolo said it seems like except for the news media, nothing has happened, adding that it's her home.

The council held its second reading Monday with public comment, but it was a quasi-judicial hearing, meaning council members acted as a panel of judges applying existing zoning rules to a specific property and making decisions based strictly on sworn testimony and factual evidence, not public opinion. The Mucciolos spoke at the meeting voicing their concerns, but they feel the council left them unheard and are now searching for answers. Margaret Mucciolo said maybe they can make the process change until it's logical, transparent, caring, and provides hope for people.

The Mucciolos say they will be exploring any kind of appeal process to change this outcome or to change the next one. Joseph Mucciolo asked where they go from here and whether they can make an objection and have this looked at again. The couple says their little piece of paradise is under threat from the rezoning decision that will allow commercial development on what is currently a wooded lot directly behind their property.

cards.headline: Rising insurance costs emerge as key Florida midterm election issue, study finds
cards.teaser: A new study shows 65% of Florida voters say rising insurance costs are making them more likely to vote in the 2026 midterm elections.
cards.body:
The cost of homeowners insurance is becoming a key political issue as the 2026 midterm elections approach, according to a new study from online insurance marketplace Insurify. The study found 58% of Americans say rising home insurance costs are making them more likely to vote in the 2026 elections. In Florida, that number climbs to 65%. Insurify economist Julia Taliesin said the study examined whether any connection exists between the political environment and insurance regulation in some states.

Insurify puts the Florida statewide average premium at $8,292, with a modest 2% increase expected this year. The study found 84% of Florida respondents plan to vote in the 2026 midterms, with 72% of Florida respondents being homeowners. Among Florida homeowners, 49% reported their home insurance premiums increased in the last 12 months. Additionally, 57% of Florida respondents feel negative about the state of the economy and 71% believe elections affect home insurance costs in their state. According to state leaders, reforms on insurance litigation have led to stable and in many cases lower rates, as more companies enter Florida adding to competition. Yet in many parts of the state, including South Florida, insurance premiums have risen as inflation and home values have increased. Republican state leaders this year have been leading the charge for property tax reform as a new affordability target. Taliesin said insurance complexity may be driving that political shift in focus, noting it demonstrates what is easiest to shift where leaders can focus and get maybe the biggest result.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce planning board reviews Causeway Cove high-rise proposal that would exceed city height limits
cards.body:
The Fort Pierce Planning Board reviewed the Causeway Cove development project on Monday, a proposal that includes five high-rise buildings off Seaway Drive, with the tallest standing 17 stories and 192 feet tall. That height is more than four times the city's current height limit. The project also calls for two hotels and more than 70,000 square feet of retail space.

The development qualifies under the Live Local Act, a state law passed in 2023 that allows developers to bypass height and density restrictions as long as they set aside 40% of units for affordable housing for at least 30 years. The project includes more than 900 apartments and condos, with 365 of those designated as affordable housing. The planning board met to review the plans as neighbors packed the chamber.

Buster Brewster, a boater at Causeway Cove Marina, said he worries the project will change the character of the area. "We're going to put this big old conglomerate up here, and I'm just afraid it's going to take away from the beauty of this place," Brewster said. Dennis Fein attended the meeting and raised concerns about traffic. "Nobody's thought this out. You're going to have massive traffic jams. Nobody's going to be able to get on the island, off the island," Fein said. City Planning Director Kev Freeman said developers must add traffic mitigation efforts and any required intersection or access improvements.

City Commissioner Michael Broderick said the city has no authority over whether the project is approved. "The city does not have a play here. We do not have a position in this. This is regulated by the state of Florida in the entirety. The city has been eliminated from the process," Broderick said. City commissioners are scheduled to hear a review of the project as the next step in the process.

hero.headline: World Cup semifinals set with England facing Argentina and Spain meeting France
hero.teaser: England and Argentina advanced to the World Cup semifinals after weekend quarterfinal victories over Norway and Switzerland, completing the final four along with France and Spain.
hero.body:
England defeated Norway in the quarterfinals with Jude Bellingham netting twice to inspire his team past Erling Haaland's squad. The 23-year-old has scored six goals in the competition, matching teammate Harry Kane. Argentina advanced with help from Julián Alvarez, who scored in extra time to help the team through to the semifinal. The match also featured a controversial VAR call. The four highest-ranked teams reached the semifinals despite a tournament full of underdog success stories and surprise results.

England has not felt comfortable in any of the games so far this tournament, starting with a 4-2 win against Croatia before scraping their way to this point. England was last in a World Cup semifinal in 2018 but lost on that occasion to Croatia. France faces Spain in one semifinal, with France considered by many to be the tournament favorite. Kylian Mbappé has been superb, with his pace and directness proving highly effective. He is supported by Ousmane Dembélé and other attackers. Spain beat France in the semifinals of Euro 2024, a tournament it went on to win, and also beat France in the Nations League last year. The World Cup final takes place on July 19.

cards.headline: Linda Noskova wins Wimbledon after recovering from blown match points in all-Czech final
cards.teaser: Linda Noskova overcame Karolina Muchova 6-2, 5-7, 6-3 on Saturday to win her first Grand Slam trophy, becoming the third Czech woman in four years to win Wimbledon.
cards.body:
The 21-year-old Noskova recovered from a second-set meltdown in which she wasted five match points to defeat Muchova in an all-Czech final at the All England Club. Noskova became the third Czech woman in four years to win the grass-court major, after Marketa Vondrousova in 2023 and Barbora Krejcikova in 2024.

Petra Kvitova, who won Wimbledon in 2011 and 2014, was in attendance, as was the greatest Czech-born player of them all, Martina Navratilova, who won a record nine singles titles at the All England Club. Navratilova looked on from the Royal Box, where she was seated next to Kate, the Princess of Wales, who was due to present the Venus Rosewater Dish trophy to Noskova. Muchova and Noskova played doubles together at the 2024 Paris Olympics and finished fourth.

cards.headline: Jannik Sinner beats Alexander Zverev to win second consecutive Wimbledon title
cards.teaser: Top-ranked Jannik Sinner defeated Alexander Zverev 6-7, 7-6, 6-3, 6-4 on Sunday at the All England Club for his fifth Grand Slam title and second straight Wimbledon championship.
cards.body:
Top-ranked Jannik Sinner beat Alexander Zverev 6-7 (7), 7-6 (2), 6-3, 6-4 Sunday for his second consecutive title at the All England Club after his German opponent appeared bothered by a knee issue following a slip to the grass on a key point in the third set. When Sinner ripped a forehand winner up the line on his first match point, the Italian dropped to the grass on his back in celebration. Sinner's fifth Grand Slam title came in his first tournament since a second-round meltdown at the French Open, when he wilted in a Paris heat wave. It was Sinner's 10th straight victory over Zverev, who was coming off his first Grand Slam title at the French Open. A year ago, Sinner beat Carlos Alcaraz in the final at the All England Club after wasting three match points against his rival in the Roland Garros final.

The top two seeds appeared perfectly matched until Zverev earned his first break point of the match at 3-3 in the third set, 2 hours and 42 minutes in. Sinner produced a drop shot and Zverev slipped and appeared to hyper-extend his right knee as he attempted to change directions behind the baseline. Zverev grasped his knee in apparent discomfort and Sinner went around the net and helped his opponent up off the grass. Zverev quickly resumed playing but appeared slightly hampered and slung his racket across the baseline in frustration when he missed a forehand and handed Sinner the first break of the match and a 5-3 lead in the third. Despite the defeat in the final, Zverev will leapfrog Alcaraz into the No. 2 spot in the rankings on Monday.

hero.headline: Florida Democrats point to special-election wins, target Republican supermajorities in 2026
hero.body:
Florida Democrats say recent special-election victories prove they can break Republican supermajorities in the state Legislature in 2026. Party leaders on Monday outlined their strategy during a virtual briefing, pointing to more than 30 local and special-election flips since the 2024 election, more than 3,000 volunteers, increased candidate recruitment and an advantage in requests for vote-by-mail ballots. Florida Democratic Party Chair Nikki Fried said the Republican supermajority in the Legislature is breakable. The party's tally includes local offices and recent legislative special elections, not 30 seats in the Florida Legislature. Fried credited the party's Pendulum Project, a year-round organizing operation designed to maintain voter contact between major elections. Democrats are also counting on a political pattern that has helped opposition parties in past midterm elections, as voters often punish the party controlling the White House.

Democrats are building their campaign around affordability issues, blaming nearly three decades of Republican control for rising costs in housing, property insurance, healthcare and everyday living expenses. The party's candidates will challenge a Republican-backed property-tax amendment headed to voters, arguing that cutting local-government revenue could threaten services or shift costs elsewhere. Fried said Republicans could have reduced the cost of living through the legislative process instead of targeting local governments. Republicans have promoted the measure as relief for homeowners facing higher tax bills, while Democrats argue it does not address property-insurance premiums and could squeeze funding for police, fire departments, roads and parks.

The climb remains steep for Democrats. Gov. Ron DeSantis defeated Democrat Charlie Crist by roughly 19 percentage points in 2022. Two years later, Trump carried Florida over Kamala Harris by about 13 points, the largest Republican presidential margin in the state since 1988. Republicans have built a voter-registration advantage of more than 1.5 million. As of May 31, Florida had about 5.54 million active registered Republicans and 4.03 million Democrats, according to the state Division of Elections. Another 3.32 million voters were registered without a party affiliation. Republicans remain at or above the two-thirds threshold needed for supermajority power in both legislative chambers. Political analyst Susan MacManus said Democrats must generate enthusiasm among supporters who have skipped recent elections while winning a sizable share of unaffiliated voters.

Democrats will continue making their case at Leadership Blue, the state party's annual gathering, scheduled for July 17 through 19 at Disney's Coronado Springs Resort in Lake Buena Vista. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg will deliver the keynote address at the July 18 gala. Senate Democratic Leader-designate Tracie Davis said the party has put in place the programs needed to capitalize and break supermajorities.

cards.headline: Florida man loses roof to Hurricane Milton months after paying off home, faces bills without insurance
cards.teaser: A Florida homeowner paid off his house only to have Hurricane Milton tear off his roof two months later, leaving him to cover repair costs without home insurance.
cards.body:
A Florida man paid off his house only for Hurricane Milton to tear off his roof two months later. Without home insurance, he was left to foot the bill for the damage. The incident highlights the consequences facing Florida homeowners who go without coverage as insurance costs continue to rise across the state.

The case illustrates the difficult choices Florida residents face between paying high insurance premiums and risking catastrophic out-of-pocket expenses when hurricanes strike. Hurricane Milton caused significant damage across areas of Florida, with uninsured homeowners bearing the full cost of repairs.

Margaret Mucciolo said the setting is what drew them to the property. She saw the beautiful setting and told the real estate agent to get ready to make an offer because it just felt like home. It was their backyard, the views of nature, and a sense of quiet relaxation that pushed them to purchase. Joseph Mucciolo said in six months or a year, it's going to be gone.

In a unanimous vote, the Port St. Lucie City Council approved changing the lot behind their yard where trees currently stand to be rezoned from residential to commercial. The council says the change is necessary to reduce traffic in the neighborhood. One council member said adding commercial closer to neighborhoods reduces the length of trips, which reduces overall traffic because if commercial is closer to you, your trips are shorter and it reduces the burden on the overall network. The two spoke at Monday's meeting, voicing their concerns, but they feel the council left them unheard. The council held its second reading Monday. While there was public comment, it was a quasi-judicial hearing, meaning council members act as a panel of judges, applying existing zoning rules to a specific property and making decisions based strictly on sworn testimony and factual evidence, not public opinion. They say they will be exploring any kind of appeal process to change this outcome or to change the next one.

cards.headline: Fire crews extinguish pickup truck fire on Florida's Turnpike in St. Lucie County
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County Fire District crews responded to a vehicle fire Monday morning on Florida's Turnpike Northbound near Mile Marker 175.
cards.body: Firefighters from St. Lucie County Fire District responded Monday morning to a vehicle fire on Florida's Turnpike Northbound near Mile Marker 175. Firefighters arrived to find a fully involved Ford F-250 pickup truck on the shoulder of the interstate. Crews initiated an aggressive fire attack, bringing the fire under control while working alongside the Florida Highway Patrol to maintain a safe scene for motorists. Traffic was temporarily impacted as firefighters extinguished the fire and secured the scene. No additional vehicles were involved. The cause of the fire is under investigation.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie Opens Registration for Free City University Program
cards.teaser:
Registration is now open for Port St. Lucie City University, a free nine-session program designed to help residents better understand how their local government operates.

Classes
cards.body:
Registration is now open for Port St. Lucie City University, a free nine-session program designed to help residents better understand how their local government operates.

Classes begin Wednesday, Aug. 12, and will be held from **5:30 to 8:30 p.m. in the Council Chambers at Port St. Lucie City Hall**, located at 121 SW Port St. Lucie Blvd.

Participants will learn about City departments, municipal services and the decision-making processes that shape the community. The program also gives residents opportunities to meet City staff, ask questions and gain a closer look at the work involved in operating one of Florida's largest cities.

Residents who complete the course will receive a certificate of completion and may also choose to become a City Ambassador, helping share information about City programs and services throughout the community.

City University is intended to encourage civic engagement while strengthening connections between residents and local government. Since the program began in 2016, more than 600 residents have participated.

**Enrollment is limited to 160 participants.**

Residents who are unable to attend the in-person classes can also access City U on Demand, which offers a more flexible way to learn about Port St. Lucie government and municipal operations.

hero.headline: Jupiter Inlet Lighthouse offers 165 years of history with 105-step climb to panoramic views
hero.teaser: The Jupiter Inlet Lighthouse, built in 1860, offers visitors a 105-step climb to panoramic views of the Atlantic Ocean, Jupiter Inlet, and Loxahatchee and Indian rivers.
hero.body:
The Jupiter Inlet Lighthouse stands as a red brick tower at the base of the Jupiter Inlet on Florida's Atlantic coast, constructed in 1860 and operating continuously for 165 years as both an active navigational aid and a public attraction. The historic structure has guided mariners since before the Civil War while welcoming visitors who climb to its observation gallery for sweeping views of the surrounding waterways and coastline. The tower's design requires visitors to follow the same path lighthouse keepers took throughout history to maintain operations.

Reaching the observation gallery at the top of the lighthouse requires ascending 105 steps up a narrow spiral staircase that winds through the interior of the brick tower. This route follows the same path that lighthouse keepers climbed night after night to maintain the powerful Fresnel lens that projected light across the water to passing ships. The spiral staircase leads upward through the tower to the gallery at the top, allowing modern visitors to retrace the steps of the early keepers who ensured the beacon remained operational throughout the decades.

The observation gallery provides panoramic views stretching across multiple waterways and the ocean. The Atlantic Ocean extends to the east, while below the tower, the turquoise waters of the Jupiter Inlet converge with the Loxahatchee and Indian rivers. Visitors at this elevated vantage point can watch boats glide through the channel as sea breezes sweep across the observation area. The commanding perspective reveals why this location proved ideal for a lighthouse, offering clear sightlines across the coastal landscape and waterways that allowed keepers to monitor maritime traffic and project the beacon across miles of ocean.

The museum grounds preserve more than just the tower itself. Restored historic buildings chronicle the lighthouse's journey from its construction before the Civil War through its years as an active Coast Guard station. These structures provide information about the lighthouse's role in regional maritime history and offer details about the daily lives of the keepers who operated the station. The site maintains the supporting buildings that allowed the lighthouse station to function across more than a century and a half of continuous service, preserving the complete story of this working navigational aid that has marked the Florida coastline for generations of mariners.
